doe-osti-3366428-energy-program-innovati:
Syracuse University's final report for DOE award DE-EE0009606, led by Ian Shapiro with Tamara Rosanio, closes the EPIC Buildings program, which ran October 2021 to June 2025. The program built a Central New York innovation cluster for grid-interactive efficient buildings: buildings that adjust energy use in conversation with the grid. The aim was a durable regional hardware ecosystem supporting a net-zero 2050 transition.

As an Energy Program Innovation Cluster, the project combined university research with company support, growing startups and prototypes around building technologies. The final report, submitted October 30, 2025, summarizes the cluster's activities and outcomes for the Office of Technology Transitions. Regional clusters like this one test whether clean building innovation can take root outside the usual coastal technology hubs.
podcast-joerogan-CnMWWRV7oeQ:
Comedian Sam Tripoli brings his conspiracy-laced act to episode 1852 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Tripoli hosts shows built on hidden-history claims, and his stand-up treats every official story as suspect. With Rogan, a friend and fellow traveler, he lets the theories run.

The talk hops across famous cover-up claims, secret groups, and the jokes Tripoli builds on top of them. Rogan joins in where the stories grab him and razzes his guest where they do not. The episode is part comedy hang, part fringe briefing, and it shows the social side of the show at full ease.
podcast-joerogan-Rx8BcDThVeQ:
Sam Tripoli returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2366, another round of conspiracy comedy at full tilt. Tripoli, host of the Tin Foil Hat podcast, treats every official story as a dare. His friendship with Rogan keeps the rants warm as well as wild.

Tripoli fires off his latest theories on secret groups, hidden tech, and staged events. Rogan laughs, argues, and feeds him new material from the week's news. The episode runs on chemistry more than on proof. Listeners who enjoy the laughing, questioning side of the show get Tripoli in full flow.
podcast-tuckercarlson-AKh4txSD0eQ:
Journalist Glenn Greenwald joins Tucker Carlson in a grave mood on the Russia war. Carlson calls the outgoing team's move the most evil act he has seen. Ukraine was cleared to strike deep inside Russia.

He warns the move hands the next leaders a nuclear risk. He also argues that Putin lacks the total power many assume. Russian politics, he says, is complex and lively. The title warns of blackmailed leaders at home. The episode is a dark brief against escalation, from two men who distrust official war talk. Both men end more alarmed than they began.
podcast-tuckercarlson-awZ7PYrofEQ:
Scottish historian and broadcaster Neil Oliver joins Tucker Carlson for a sweeping talk on banks, empires, and modern crises. Oliver argues that banking power quietly took over the fate of nations. The conversation ranges across World War II, Brexit, and COVID from his coastal Scottish view.

Oliver lays out how finance, in his telling, bent empires and governments to its will. He shares his dissenting takes on the war, Britain's exit from Europe, and the pandemic years. Carlson finds a kindred skeptic across the Atlantic. Questioning viewers get a broad, poetic brief against the modern order.
podcast-tuckercarlson-gBgRgn3ENeQ:
Tucker Carlson delivers a full speech on the America First movement at a Charlie Kirk event. He opens with jokes about walking out to the crowd. Then he turns on calls to shun speakers.

He laughs, he says, at demands to deplatform people at such an event. The title calls that push a new agenda on the right. Carlson defends open debate inside the movement. He urges the crowd to reject loyalty tests. The tape preserves a key moment in the right's internal fight, in the speaker's own words. The crowd hears the charge and roars back.
podcast-tuckercarlson-uBGNJ4m-IeQ:
Mike Rowe, host of Dirty Jobs, talks with Tucker Carlson about the real dangers of AI. Rowe has spent years championing skilled trades and the dignity of hard physical work. His take on the machine age is grounded in that mission, not in tech hype.

Rowe argues the deeper danger is a culture that stops valuing work done with hands. He warns that AI hype pushes young people away from trades the country desperately needs. Carlson asks what happens when no one can fix, build, or farm. Working and thoughtful viewers get a grounded warning from television's most famous laborer.
